source: Hansson (SEP) Logic of Belief Revision
finding: AGM theory (Alchourron, Gardenfors, Makinson 1985) models a belief state as a deductively closed set K. Three operations: expansion (add), contraction (remove), revision (add and keep consistent). Revision has six basic postulates: Closure, Success, Inclusion, Vacuity, Consistency, Extensionality.
numbers: Six basic revision postulates plus two supplementary (Superexpansion, Subexpansion). Contraction has six basic (Closure, Success, Inclusion, Vacuity, Extensionality, Recovery) plus two supplementary (Conjunctive inclusion, Conjunctive overlap).
limits: Idealised: beliefs are closed under logic, so it is for a logically omniscient agent. Success (the input must be believed afterward) is the most disputed.
agent_relevance: S5 Revise can be read as AGM revision on a finite set of candidate claims. Success says the failing check always wins; that matches G2 (revise from real output).

source: Hansson (SEP) Logic of Belief Revision
finding: Revision and contraction are interdefinable. Levi identity: revise by p = contract by not-p, then expand by p. So the real question is which beliefs to drop when contracting.
numbers: K*p = (K minus not-p) + p. Attributed to Gardenfors 1981 and Levi 1977.
limits: Contraction is not unique: many different maximal consistent subsets can be kept. The theory alone does not pick one.
agent_relevance: Our S5 only needs the contraction step: which member of the candidate set to give up. Revision then adds the failing output as a new fact.

source: Hansson (SEP) Logic of Belief Revision
finding: Epistemic entrenchment (Gardenfors 1988; Gardenfors and Makinson 1988) is the preference order that picks what to drop. Five postulates: Transitivity, Dominance, Conjunctiveness, Minimality, Maximality. Contraction rule: q stays in K minus p iff q is in K and p is strictly less entrenched than (p or q), or p is a tautology.
numbers: Entrenchment-based contraction coincides with transitively relational partial meet contraction. Severe withdrawal changes the keep condition to p < q.
limits: Entrenchment must be supplied from outside; AGM does not say where it comes from.
agent_relevance: Entrenchment is the slot where our test results go: a claim that passed more held-out checks is more entrenched and is dropped last.

source: Hansson (SEP) Logic of Belief Revision
finding: Grove (1988) gave a semantic model: a system of spheres around the current belief set. Revision by p takes the narrowest sphere that intersects the p-worlds. This matches transitively relational partial meet revision. Katsuno and Mendelzon (1992) separated revision (learn that the world was different from believed) from update (the world changed).
numbers: Representation theorems: postulates hold iff the operator is built from a total preorder over worlds.
limits: Revision vs update matters: a failed check on a static task is revision; a changing environment is update.
agent_relevance: Our tasks are static puzzles, so revision, not update, is the right model. Plausibility ordering over candidate answers is a natural data structure.

source: Hansson (SEP) Logic of Belief Revision
finding: Recovery postulate is the standard counterexample target. Hansson's Cleopatra case: learn she had a child, contract that, then re-learn she had a child, and you should not get back the belief that she had a son or a daughter.
numbers: Recovery says adding back what you removed restores the old set. Counterexample in SEP Section 2.3. Fix: withdrawal operators that drop Recovery.
limits: Disputed since the 1980s; many authors keep it for belief sets and drop it for belief bases.
agent_relevance: Do not require the agent to restore a dropped hypothesis when the contradicting check is later removed; do not rely on Recovery.

source: Hansson (SEP) Logic of Belief Revision
finding: Belief bases (Hansson): revise a finite list of stated beliefs instead of a closed set. Postulates for base partial meet contraction: Success, Inclusion, Relevance, Uniformity. Relevance replaces Recovery. Kernel contraction cuts the smallest sets that entail the unwanted claim. Consolidation (Hansson 1991) restores consistency.
numbers: Representation theorem for partial meet contraction on bases (Hansson 1999).
limits: Bases are syntax-sensitive: two equivalent bases can revise differently. This is a feature for agents, a flaw for logicians.
agent_relevance: A scaffold holds a finite list of claims, not a closed theory, so base revision is the matching formalism.

source: Hansson (SEP) Logic of Belief Revision
finding: Iterated revision. Darwiche and Pearl (1997) postulates DP1-DP4 (called C1-C4 elsewhere) constrain what happens on repeated revision. DP1: if q implies p, revising by p then q equals revising by q. DP2: if q implies not-p, same. DP3 and DP4 say a past input is kept (DP3) or not newly refuted (DP4) when later input is compatible.
numbers: Core idea: revising by p should leave the order among p-worlds and among not-p worlds unchanged and only move one block relative to the other.
limits: Original AGM does not say how the order itself changes, so it cannot be iterated.
agent_relevance: Direct constraint on repeated S5 rounds: later evidence should not erase the ordering built from earlier checks beyond what the new fact forces.

source: Hansson (SEP) Logic of Belief Revision
finding: Gardenfors impossibility (1986, 1987): the Ramsey test for conditionals is incompatible with plausible revision postulates. Responses: drop the Ramsey test (Rott 1986) or exclude conditionals from the belief set (Levi).
numbers: Brief treatment in SEP section 7.6.
limits: Result is about conditional beliefs, not plain facts.
agent_relevance: Warns against storing if-then rules inside the same revisable set as facts.

source: Booth and Meyer (2006) Admissible and Restrained Revision
finding: Darwiche-Pearl postulates C1-C4 in words: C1, a more specific later input makes the earlier one redundant. C2, two contradictory inputs: the later one prevails. C3, evidence kept after later evidence that the current state already supports. C4, no input can refute itself. Boutilier natural revision (the most conservative DP operator) is too stingy: it can ignore the penultimate input.
numbers: Admissible revision class keeps the second-to-last input in play. Nayak lexicographic revision is the least conservative admissible operator. New restrained revision is the most conservative admissible operator. Restrained revision equals natural revision preceded by Papini backwards revision.
limits: Choice among operators is still open; the authors call for context-based choice.
agent_relevance: Menu of three iterated policies for a scaffold: natural (change as little as possible), restrained (conservative but remembers the last two checks), lexicographic (newest evidence outranks all older).

source: Aravanis (2026) Machine Learning as Iterated Belief Change a la Darwiche and Pearl
finding: Lexicographic revision (Nayak) makes every p-world strictly more plausible than every not-p world and keeps the order inside each block. Moderate contraction is the contraction partner. Both satisfy Darwiche-Pearl. Full-meet revision has known flaws and loses all prior ordering.
numbers: Worked examples on binary feed-forward networks, including an MNIST example where classification accuracy rises step by step to 100% as the belief set is revised.
limits: Theory paper on small binary networks; no LLM. The accuracy figure comes from an illustrative example, not a benchmark.
agent_relevance: Shows that a training-like sequence of corrections can be seen as a chain of DP-compliant revisions. Supports treating repeated S5 as ordered revision with memory.

source: Friedman and Halpern (2001) Belief Revision: A Critique
finding: The AGM postulates are under-specified about what the agent models. Success (believe the last input) and Vacuity (no change if the input is already consistent) were called beyond controversy by Rott (1989). The authors show both fail when beliefs include beliefs about the agent's own epistemic state, and when observations are only believed, not known.
numbers: Example: a scientist who believes heavy objects fall faster drops a 5 kg book and a 500 mg novel, sees them land together. One observation does not force acceptance of weight-independence.
limits: Philosophical critique; no experiments.
agent_relevance: Supports G3 and G4: one observation is not automatically accepted. Treat a failed check as evidence with a strength, not as certain.

source: Chopra, Ghose and Meyer (2002) Iterated revision and the axiom of recovery
finding: Epistemic states (preference structures), not belief sets, are the right object for iterated revision. The authors keep a recovery-like axiom inside this framework and argue that the contested DP postulate C2 is captured by recovery-like intuitions.
numbers: Representation theorem links the semantic conditions to the syntactic ones.
limits: Theory only.
agent_relevance: Keep a record of why each belief was dropped so a dropped hypothesis can be restored if the blocking check is later shown wrong.

source: Georgatos (2000) Entrenchment Relations: A Uniform Approach to Nonmonotonicity
finding: Gabbay-style nonmonotonic consequence relations reduce to a family called entrenchment relations, a direct generalisation of epistemic entrenchment. This ties belief revision to default reasoning.
numbers: Reduction proven in the paper; no empirical numbers.
limits: Theory only.
agent_relevance: Links to the parallel subfield on non-monotonic and default logic: one entrenchment order can serve both.

source: Sauerwald and Beierle (2022) Iterated Belief Change, Computationally
finding: Iterative belief revision is Turing complete, even when the Darwiche-Pearl postulates hold. A sequence of DP-compliant revisions can simulate any Turing machine.
numbers: Main theorem by encoding machine steps in ranking functions.
limits: Proof uses unbounded, countable epistemic states; for finite bounded agents it is not a practical limit but shows no general decision shortcut exists.
agent_relevance: Postulates alone do not make iterated revision cheap or safe. The agent needs a fixed budget and best-so-far rule (G6).

source: Wilie et al. (2024) Belief Revision: The Adaptability of Large Language Models Reasoning
finding: Belief-R tests revision with Byrne-style suppression tasks built from ATOMIC. After a first conclusion, a third premise either defeats it (Belief Update, BU) or does not (Belief Maintain, BM). About 30 models failed to revise well.
numbers: Set sizes: 1912 basic items, 1074 BU and 670 BM items (table as read; 1744 items with three premises). Models above 6B params exceed 75% on the basic step; instruction-tuned from 2.7B reach 90%. Most open models score near 0% BU-Acc. Best large LLMs reach at most about 50% on BREU, the mean of BU and BM.
limits: Only modus ponens and modus tollens triggers; new premise is the only trigger. Table row labels were partly garbled in the text extraction.
agent_relevance: Direct test of the S5 decision: update or hold. Plain models often fail it, so the program, not the model, should decide revise-or-keep.

source: Wilie et al. (2024) Belief-R, per-model rows
finding: Large models show a sharp trade-off: strong at maintaining, weak at updating. Chain of thought and plan-and-solve do not fix it.
numbers: Direct prompting rows (BU / BM / BREU): GPT-4 Turbo 19.65 / 82.69 / 51.17; Claude 3 Sonnet 9.40 / 88.66 / 49.03; Mixtral 8x22B 35.38 / 36.57 / 35.98. Plan-and-solve added only about 1 point of BREU on average.
limits: Row-to-model mapping read from a two-column text dump, so verify against the paper before quoting.
agent_relevance: Reasoning prompts do not teach when to revise. Put the revise signal (check failed) in code.

source: Wilie et al. (2024) Belief-R, difficulty split
finding: Revision is harder with modus tollens than modus ponens, and for mental-state effects than for event effects (models lean to keep beliefs). Adding a distracting third premise lowers basic inference accuracy.
numbers: BREU is lower on modus tollens; BU-Acc is higher but BM-Acc much lower there, so decisions are less clear-cut.
limits: Synthetic premises from an LLM; human agreement checked on a quality sample.
agent_relevance: Backward reasoning from a failed output to the culprit is the hard part; show the model the failing output (G2).

source: Hase et al. (2024) Fundamental Problems With Model Editing
finding: Model editing is belief revision. The paper lists 12 open problems and builds a Wikidata-based testbed where an ideal Bayesian agent gives the gold posterior. The authors say AGM-like theory handles only full belief and no single accepted theory says which beliefs to give up.
numbers: Test model: Mistral-7B-style, trained from scratch, memorises over 90% of 100k true facts.
quote: model editing is essentially belief revision, a storied problem in philosophy that has eluded succinct solutions for decades
limits: Small synthetic world; one architecture.
agent_relevance: Gold-standard idea is reusable: compare revisions to an exact Bayesian posterior on a toy domain.

source: Hase et al. (2024) Fundamental Problems With Model Editing, results
finding: Edits fix the edited fact but do not propagate. Where the correct downstream answer should change, edits reach almost no accuracy. Logical coherence also fails: the edited model does not treat negation and conjunction consistently.
numbers: Table 4, edit requests with downstream answer change: edited fact accuracy 0.90 to 1.00; downstream fact 0.97 to 0.01 (a -0.96 change); probabilistic coherence MAE downstream 0.34 to 0.59. All edits: downstream 0.93 to 0.76.
limits: Edits are weight edits (fine-tuning), not in-context revision.
agent_relevance: Revising a conclusion without revising its dependents leaves the set inconsistent. After a revision, re-check dependent claims in code.

source: Hofweber et al. (2025) Are Language Models Rational? Coherence Norms and Belief Revision
finding: Argues that coherence norms apply to some language models and not others. Introduces the Minimal Assent Connection and defines model credence from next-token probabilities. Belief revision norms are tied to the synchronic ones.
numbers: No benchmark numbers; conceptual paper.
limits: Philosophical; credence-from-logits is a proposal, not a validated measure.
agent_relevance: Gives a way to read a model's confidence as an entrenchment proxy, but G4 warns that agreement is not proof.

source: Dhanda (2026) DeltaLogic
finding: Minimal premise edits (insert, delete, replace) on FOLIO and ProofWriter items. Three failure types: inertia (keeps stale answer), over-flip (revises under an irrelevant edit), abstention. Initial reasoning skill does not predict revision skill.
numbers: Qwen3-1.7B: 0.667 initial, 0.467 revised, inertia 0.600 (30 episodes). Qwen3-4B: 0.650 initial, 0.450 revised, inertia 0.600 (20). Phi-4-mini: 0.950 initial, 0.850 revised (20). Qwen3-0.6B: abstains on all revised items.
limits: Tiny samples (20 to 30 episodes), small models, workshop paper.
agent_relevance: Gives the right metrics for our log: inertia rate and over-flip rate, separate from first-pass accuracy.

source: Mannan et al. (2026) AI scientists produce results without reasoning scientifically
finding: More than 25,000 agent runs across 8 science domains. The base model, not the scaffold, drives behaviour. Agents rarely revise on refutation.
numbers: Base model 41.4% of explained variance vs 1.5% for the scaffold. Evidence ignored in 68% of traces; beliefs never updated in 71%; refutation-driven revision in 26%; untested claims in 53% (63% in hypothesis-driven domains); convergent multi-test evidence in 7%. Persists when given near-complete successful trajectories.
quote: evidence is ignored in 68% of traces, refutation-driven belief revision occurs in 26%
limits: Trace labels were produced by an annotation pipeline; domain mix includes workflow tasks where revision is not needed.
agent_relevance: Strong support for forcing revision in code: scaffold prompts alone did not raise revision (scaffold 1.5% of variance).

source: Park (2026) Kumiho: graph-native memory with AGM semantics
finding: An agent memory with immutable versioned revisions and typed edges, argued to satisfy AGM basic postulates and Hansson base postulates (Relevance, Core-Retainment). Recovery is rejected on purpose because old versions are immutable. K*7 and K*8 left open.
numbers: Automated check of 49 scenarios over 7 postulates: 100% pass. LoCoMo: 0.447 four-category F1 (n=1,540), 0.565 with adversarial (n=1,986); adversarial refusal 97.5% (n=446). LoCoMo-Plus: 93.3% judge accuracy.
limits: Author-written tests of own implementation; propositional ground triples only; self-reported benchmarks. 100% compliance is operational, not a proof for LLM content.
agent_relevance: Practical template: supersedes edges and a current-tag pointer give best-so-far plus an audit trail.

source: Singh (2026) When Does Belief-Based Agent Memory Help? (Nous)
finding: Bayesian belief updating in agent memory is inert on LoCoMo (naive last-write-wins ties it), because ordinary dialogue rarely holds contradictions. It pays off only with a per-claim reliability signal.
numbers: Synthetic contradiction benchmark, 60 scenarios, 5 regimes: realistic macro score 100 (reliability-weighted Bayes) vs 67 last-write-wins vs 46 frequency vs 90 append-and-retrieve. Adversarial regime (confidence inverted): Bayes scores 0. Token-F1 vs LLM-judge on LoCoMo: 32.45 vs 59.97.
limits: Synthetic data; confidence-correctness link built in by design in 4 of 5 regimes; three-conversation ablation.
agent_relevance: Entrenchment from stated confidence helps only when confidence tracks truth; in code-verified checks, use test results, not the model's hedges (G3, G4).

source: Abtahi et al. (2026) MEDLEY-BENCH
finding: Benchmark of prompted belief revision under private self-review and social disagreement: 35 models, 12 families, 130 instances. Rubric component 'Evaluation' was lowest in 30 of 35 models. Sensitivity to manipulated consensus labels ranged from near zero to large.
numbers: Adversarial study of 11 models: largest label-sensitive shifts +11.6 and +7.3 points for two models. Human rubric agreement, quadratic weighted kappa 0.389 (24 response-items).
limits: Proof-of-concept release; authors flag judge-severity and pipeline confounds; v1.5 rerun planned. Low human agreement.
agent_relevance: Models can be pushed to revise by social cues rather than evidence. G4 and G5: hide majority and authorship when judging.

source: Bertolazzi et al. (2026) FalsifyBench
finding: Wason 2-4-6 style rule discovery with 12 LLMs. Reasoning models beat instruction-tuned ones. Success is driven by negative testing (trying to falsify), not by confirmation.
numbers: 12 LLMs; no model near optimal. Numbers not read beyond abstract and introduction.
limits: Only the abstract and intro were read; not counted as opened.
agent_relevance: Hypothesis revision depends on seeking disconfirming tests; relevant to the S5 trigger.

source: Wilie et al. (2024) Belief-R, framing and limits
finding: Authors state the limits: only logic-driven change, new premises as trigger, no re-evaluation of old knowledge without new input. The task follows Byrne (1989) suppression experiments in humans, where people withdraw a modus ponens conclusion when an additional condition is given.
numbers: Human majority choices in Byrne (1989) and Byrne et al. (1999) were used as the target answers.
limits: Human numbers were not re-read here; only cited as the target.
agent_relevance: The human baseline is selective withdrawal; models over-hold or over-flip.
